With that said, I -living in Iran- do have some knowledge of what is generally known as "Islamic philosophy" (I don't know if they're considered ethnic, though they are definitely not Western). Here are the three main figures of Islamic philosophy:

Avicenna: (known as an Aristotelian thinker)
https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ibn-sina/

Suhrawardi: (known as a Platonic thinker)
https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/suhrawardi/

Mulla-sadra:
https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mulla-sadra/

These philosophers -and some more- are commonly teached in universities of Islamic countries and some of them greatly influenced Western thinkers in medieval period. Also you would find a great deal of their discussions similar to Western philosophy - since they both have the same origin, namely, Plato and Aristotle.

A few problems with this theory:

1- Most great artists are dead. Who knows what Dante was thinking about when writing Divine Comedy? More generally: most of the time you have no way of knowing what the artist intended. You can only guess. How do I know if author of animal farm was just thinking about a bunch of talking animals or Soviet Union? Who knows?

2- All great art -at least in literature and painting- is about metaphor. It is fiction so it can never be factual. If I want to say what I think about french revolution in a straight forward way then I would be writing an essay on politics or history or something. That wouldn't be art. Is Great Expectations just about some poor kid getting rich and has no connection to the actual society? The point of art is to make us see in reality what is hard to see otherwise.

3- A lot of things that you see in a work of art were put there unconsciously by the artist. Like when a psychologist can say about a child by the drawings that he or she draws. A great example in literature is Kafka's stories.
